title_en: Zhengzhou Erjian Company v. Wang Liangchu — dispute over breach of a public housing sale agreement
ruling_gist_en: 1. A unit owner in a condominium may only exercise the four powers of ownership over the exclusive part of the building that belongs to such owner. Without the permission of other unit owners, the property management operator, and the maintenance personnel, such owner may not exercise rights over the common parts of the building.

full_text_en:
Zhengzhou Second Construction Engineering Company v.  
Wang Liangchu — dispute over breach of agreement on sale of public housing  

【Ruling Summary】  

1. A holder of a condominium ownership right may only exercise the four powers of ownership over the exclusive-use portion of the building. Without the permission of other co-owners and the property operation manager or maintenance person of the building, the holder may not exercise rights over the common parts of the building.  

2. The unit that sold public housing bears the maintenance responsibility for the common parts of the public housing. In the housing sale agreement signed with the buyer of the public housing, in order not to increase its own maintenance burden after the housing is sold, the selling unit may include a clause that the buyer shall not engage in acts that endanger the safety of the common parts of the public housing. Such a clause does not restrict the buyer's proper exercise of his own rights and is therefore legally valid.  

Plaintiff: Henan Zhengzhou Second Construction Engineering Company, domiciled at Hongqi Road, Jinshui District, Zhengzhou City.  
Legal representative: Deng Yukun, Manager of the Company.  
Defendant: Wang Liangchu, male, 78 years old, residing at Room 11, Building 1, No. 92 Huanghe Road, Jinshui District, Zhengzhou City.  

The Plaintiff, Henan Zhengzhou Second Construction Engineering Company (hereinafter referred to as Zhengzhou Erjian Company), filed a lawsuit with the People's Court of Jinshui District, Zhengzhou City, Henan Province, against the Defendant, Wang Liangchu, over a dispute concerning breach of an agreement on the sale of public housing.  

The Plaintiff alleged: The Defendant, in violation of the agreement and without the Plaintiff's consent, took advantage of the Huanghe Road renovation project to arbitrarily open a door and a window in the housing unit he purchased from the Plaintiff, namely Room 11, Building 1, No. 92 Huanghe Road, Zhengzhou City. This conduct seriously affected the quality of Building 1 and the safety of other residents. As the builder and manager of Building 1, the Plaintiff issued a notice to the Defendant requiring him to restore the altered housing unit to its original condition, but the Defendant ignored it. The Plaintiff requested a judgment ordering the Defendant to comply with the agreement and immediately restore the arbitrarily altered housing unit to its original condition.  

The Defendant argued: 1. Although Building 1 was built by the Plaintiff, the Plaintiff has already sold the building. The Plaintiff is neither the owners' committee of Building 1, nor the property manager of Building 1, nor the owner of Building 1, and therefore has no right to sue the Defendant regarding the use of Building 1. 2. When the Plaintiff sold Room 11, Building 1 to the Defendant, the two parties did sign an agreement, and Article 6 of that agreement indeed contained provisions such as "no opening of doors or windows." Since the housing was sold, the buyer became the new owner of the housing. Pursuant to Article 71 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the General Principles of Civil Law), the owner has the right to possess, use, profit from, and dispose of his own property. Article 6 of the agreement infringes upon the buyer's ownership of the housing, violates the provisions of the General Principles of Civil Law, is an invalid clause, and has no legal binding force. The Defendant was merely exercising his ownership rights over his own housing lawfully and did not breach the agreement. The Plaintiff's lawsuit should be dismissed.  

The People's Court of Jinshui District, Zhengzhou City, found through trial:  

Building 1, No. 92 Huanghe Road, Jinshui District, Zhengzhou City, was a five-story public residential building constructed by the Plaintiff, Zhengzhou Erjian Company, at the end of 1980. Room 11 was located on the first floor and faced the street, and was allocated to the Defendant, Wang Liangchu, an employee of the company, for his residence. During the housing system reform in 1996, Zhengzhou Erjian Company sold public residential housing to its employees at a cost price of RMB 649 per square meter. After deducting discounts for length of service and other items, Wang Liangchu purchased Room 11, with a construction area of 56.82 square meters, for a price of RMB 10,540.29.  

After public housing is sold and the buyer has resided in it for five years, it may enter the market for circulation in accordance with the law. On September 1, 2000, in order to obtain the certificate of ownership required for the housing to enter the market for circulation, the Plaintiff, Zhengzhou Erjian Company, and the Defendant, Wang Liangchu, signed a supplementary "Agreement on the Sale of Public Housing." In addition to stipulating that the Defendant would own Room 11, the Agreement also provided in Article 5: After the housing is sold, Party A (Plaintiff) is responsible for normal maintenance during the warranty period stipulated by the state; after the warranty period expires, Party B (Defendant) is responsible for maintenance of the self-use parts, and Party A is responsible for maintenance of the external walls, corridors, passages, and other common parts of Building 1. Article 6 set out the management measures for the sold housing, including: (1) Without Party A's consent, Party B shall not engage in acts that change the structure of the housing, such as opening doors, windows, or building partition walls; shall not relocate equipment; and shall not add stories to the housing; otherwise, Party B shall be responsible for restoring the original condition and demolishing unauthorized constructions. (2) The sold housing shall not be leased. If Party B wishes to change the nature of the housing's use, it must obtain Party A's consent and go through the relevant procedures. (3) Party B shall take care of the common parts of the housing and shall not encroach upon the common parts of the housing, nor hinder others' normal use of the common parts of the housing.  

After the agreement was signed, the Defendant, Wang Liangchu, obtained the certificate of ownership for Room 11, Building 1. In 2004, Wang Liangchu opened a door and a window in the street-facing wall of Room 11. The Plaintiff, Zhengzhou Erjian Company, considered Wang Liangchu's conduct a breach of the agreement and, after unsuccessful persuasion, initiated this lawsuit, requesting that Wang Liangchu restore the housing to its original condition.  

The People's Court of Jinshui District, Zhengzhou City, held:  

The "Agreement on the Sale of Public Housing" signed by the parties reflected their true intentions and did not violate the law, and therefore should be recognized as legally valid. Article 8 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "A lawfully formed contract is legally binding on the parties. The parties shall perform their obligations in accordance with the agreement and shall not alter or terminate the contract without authorization." "A lawfully formed contract is protected by law." After obtaining ownership of Room 11, Building 1, the Defendant, Wang Liangchu, violated the terms of the agreement signed by the parties and, without the permission of the Plaintiff, Zhengzhou Erjian Company, arbitrarily opened doors and windows in the wall of Room 11, thereby altering the load-bearing structure of Building 1 and creating a safety hazard for the residents of the upper floors. Article 111 of the General Principles of Civil Law provides: "If a party fails to fulfill its contractual obligations or fulfills them in a manner that does not conform to the agreed conditions, the other party has the right to demand performance or to take remedial measures, and has the right to demand compensation for losses." After Wang Liangchu's breach, Zhengzhou Erjian Company had the right to demand that Wang Liangchu restore Room 11 to its original condition in accordance with Article 134, Paragraph 1, Item (5) of the General Principles of Civil Law.  

Accordingly, the People's Court of Jinshui District, Zhengzhou City, rendered judgment on September 25, 2005:  

The Defendant, Wang Liangchu, shall, within ten days after this judgment takes effect, restore the altered parts of Room 11, Building 1, No. 92 Huanghe Road, Jinshui District, Zhengzhou City, where doors and windows were arbitrarily opened, to their original condition.  

Court acceptance fee of RMB 50 shall be borne by the Defendant, Wang Liangchu.  

After the first-instance judgment was announced, Wang Liangchu refused to accept it and appealed to the Zhengzhou Intermediate People's Court, Henan Province, arguing: 1. Article 6 of the "Agreement on the Sale of Public Housing" clearly conflicts with Article 71 of the General Principles of Civil Law regarding property ownership and is therefore void. The agreement was a standard-form contract provided by the appellee. Because the parties were trading public housing and the appellant was an employee of the appellee, the appellant dared not openly reject the unreasonable clauses in the standard-form contract and therefore signed it. The first-instance court failed to ascertain the true circumstances under which the agreement was signed and erroneously recognized the invalid clauses as valid, which was an error in fact-finding. 2. Ownership of Room 11 has transferred to the appellant, and the appellee has no connection with the housing now and has no right to interfere with the appellant's disposition of his own property. 3. Whether the appellant's opening of doors and windows in Room 11 creates a safety hazard for the residents of the upper floors cannot be inferred without evidence. In the first instance, the appellee provided no evidence to prove that the appellant's opening of doors and windows would create a safety hazard for the upper-floor residents. The first-instance court inferred, without any evidence, that the appellant's opening of doors and windows created a safety hazard for the upper-floor residents; this inference was not valid. 4. Among the public housing units sold by the appellee, more than 20 households made alterations to their housing, but the appellee only sued the appellant, which was clearly unequal treatment and amounted to bullying weak groups. In sum, the first-instance judgment was erroneous, and the appellant requested that the second-instance court amend the judgment to protect his legitimate rights and interests.  

The appellee, Zhengzhou Erjian Company, argued: 1. The housing sold to the appellant by the appellee was part of a whole building. To ensure that buyers would not engage in acts endangering the safety of the whole building and the residents of the upper floors after purchasing the housing, Article 6 of the "Agreement on the Sale of Public Housing" set out certain acts that buyers could not undertake after purchasing the housing. 2. Article 58, Paragraph 1 of the Construction Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Construction enterprises shall be responsible for the quality of the construction work." Article 62, Paragraph 1 provides: "A quality warranty system shall be implemented for construction projects." Article 70 provides: "Whoever, in violation of the provisions of this Law, starts construction of a renovation project involving changes to the main structure or load-bearing structure without authorization shall be ordered to rectify the situation and may be fined; if losses are caused, the party shall bear liability for compensation; if the conduct constitutes a crime, criminal liability shall be pursued." Article 71, Paragraph 1 provides: "If a construction enterprise, in violation of the provisions of this Law, fails to take measures to eliminate hidden dangers of construction accidents, it shall be ordered to rectify the situation and may be fined; if the circumstances are serious, it shall be ordered to suspend business for rectification, its qualification grade shall be lowered, or its qualification certificate shall be revoked; if the conduct constitutes a crime, criminal liability shall be pursued." Article 75 provides: "If a construction enterprise, in violation of the provisions of this Law, fails to perform its warranty obligations or delays in performing them, it shall be ordered to rectify the situation and may be fined, and shall bear liability for compensation for losses caused by quality defects such as leakage and cracking of roofs and walls during the warranty period." Article 80 provides: "During the reasonable service life of a building, if a person suffers damage due to the substandard quality of the construction project, he has the right to claim compensation from the person responsible." The appellee was not only the construction unit but also the construction enterprise of Building 1, and was legally responsible for the warranty of Building 1. This responsibility did not cease simply because Building 1 was sold. After the appellant purchased Room 11, although he enjoyed ownership of the housing, the exercise of his rights could not be unrestricted; he had to take into account the interests of the state, society, the collective, and the lawful freedoms and rights of other citizens. The "Agreement on the Sale of Public Housing" was indeed a standard-form contract provided by the appellee, but its content complied with the relevant provisions of the Construction Law and other administrative regulations and was therefore legally valid. 3. The appellant's arbitrary opening of doors and windows on the building destroyed the originally designed load-bearing structure. This breach of contract undoubtedly created a safety hazard for the building, which is a well-known fact deducible from the rules of daily life experience and requires no proof. 4. As for how many other households had engaged in similar breaches of contract, whether the appellee chose to sue them at the same time, later, or not at all was a matter of the appellee's litigation rights and did not constitute unequal treatment or bullying of weak groups. The first-instance judgment was correct and should be affirmed.  

The Zhengzhou Intermediate People's Court, through trial, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.  

The issues in dispute in this case were: 1. Whether Article 6 of the "Agreement on the Sale of Public Housing" was legally valid. 2. Whether Wang Liangchu should bear liability for his act of opening doors and windows, and if so, what kind of liability. 3. Whether Zhengzhou Erjian Company had standing to sue Wang Liangchu for opening doors and windows in Room 11.  

The Zhengzhou Intermediate People's Court held:  

1. Building 1, No. 92 Huanghe Road, Jinshui District, Zhengzhou City, was a five-story public residential building constructed by the appellee, Zhengzhou Erjian Company. Zhengzhou Erjian Company was both the construction unit and the housing selling unit of Building 1. Any building consists of individual rooms that can be used independently, as well as common parts of the entire building, such as floors, roofs, beams, columns, internal and external walls, foundations, and water supply and drainage pipes. Article 4, Paragraph 2 of the "Interim Measures for the Administration of Maintenance and Repair of Public Housing After Sale" issued by the Ministry of Construction on June 15, 1992, provides: "The common parts of a residential building refer to load-bearing structural parts (including floors, roofs, beams, columns, internal and external walls, and foundations), external walls, stairwells, corridor passages, entrance halls, indoor bicycle parking garages, etc." Article 6 provides: "After public housing is sold, the maintenance and repair of the common parts and common facilities and equipment of the housing shall be undertaken by the housing selling unit, or the housing selling unit may, at the time of sale, entrust a real estate management unit to undertake the maintenance and repair." Pursuant to this provision, Zhengzhou Erjian Company, in Article 5 of the "Agreement on the Sale of Public Housing," clarified its maintenance responsibility for the common parts of Building 1, and, in Article 6, from the perspective of the building's maintenance person, expressly prohibited the building's users from engaging in acts that would endanger the building's safety. This provision is conducive to extending the building's service life and does not affect the proper exercise of users' rights in accordance with the law; therefore, it is a legally valid contractual clause.  

2. Room 11, sold by the appellee, Zhengzhou Erjian Company, to the appellant, Wang Liangchu, is located on the first floor of Building 1 and is a component of Building 1; it is not an independent structure. Given the architectural characteristics of the building, Wang Liangchu's ownership of Room 11 is not independent or complete ownership but rather a condominium ownership (Eigentumswohnung). A holder of condominium ownership only enjoys complete ownership, including the four powers of possession, use, profit, and disposition, over the part of the entire building that belongs exclusively to him. The common parts of the entire building are co-owned by all condominium owners of the building. The street-facing wall of Room 11 is an indispensable common part of Building 1 and cannot be exclusively owned by Wang Liangchu. By opening a door and a window in this wall without permission, Wang Liangchu not only infringed upon the common rights of other co-owners of Building 1 but also, due to his violation of Article 6 of the "Agreement on the Sale of Public Housing," should bear liability for breach of contract to Zhengzhou Erjian Company.  

3. Pursuant to Article 6 of the "Interim Measures for the Administration of Maintenance and Repair of Public Housing After Sale," although the appellee, Zhengzhou Erjian Company, is not the property management unit, the owners' committee, or the owner of Building 1, before a new property management unit takes over after the sale of Building 1, Zhengzhou Erjian Company, as the construction unit and housing selling unit of Building 1, bears the maintenance responsibility for the common parts of Building 1. By opening a door and a window in the street-facing wall of Room 11, Building 1, the appellant, Wang Liangchu, increased the maintenance burden on Zhengzhou Erjian Company and directly affected its interests. Therefore, Zhengzhou Erjian Company had the right to sue Wang Liangchu for breach of contract in accordance with the "Agreement on the Sale of Public Housing."  

In conclusion, the "Agreement on the Sale of Public Housing" reflected the true intentions of the parties and did not violate the law; it should be recognized as valid. The appellant, Wang Liangchu, breached the agreement by arbitrarily opening doors and windows in the common parts of Building 1 and should bear liability for breach of contract. Zhengzhou Erjian Company, as a party to the "Agreement on the Sale of Public Housing" and as the maintenance manager of Building 1, had standing to sue Wang Liangchu for breach of contract and to demand restoration of the original condition. The first-instance judgment was factually clear and legally correct and should be affirmed. Wang Liangchu's grounds for appeal were untenable and should be rejected. Accordingly, the Zhengzhou Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered judgment on April 24, 2006:  

Appeal dismissed; the original judgment was affirmed.  

Court acceptance fee of RMB 50 for the second instance shall be borne by the appellant, Wang Liangchu.  

This judgment is final.
